name: Fractional CO2 laser (CO2RE, Ultrapulse, SmartXide)

lead: Fractional CO2 is the heavy-duty option in laser resurfacing, used to smooth acne and surgical scars and soften deep wrinkles and photodamage. CO2RE, UltraPulse and SmartXide are common systems.

The 10,600 nm beam is absorbed by water in the skin and vaporizes microscopic columns of tissue, with untreated skin between them speeding healing. The skin then rebuilds collagen over the following months. It is among the better-studied fractional lasers, with burn-scar cohorts, acne scar studies in Asian patients and randomized trials combined with other therapies.

paras: It is performed in a clinic, often with numbing, and is usually a single session or a small series rather than a frequent routine. People plan a recovery period with redness, swelling and peeling, which is typically longer than after non-ablative lasers. Final results are judged after healing and continued collagen remodeling.

Reported risks include hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, scarring, acne and herpes outbreaks. Wikipedia notes CO2 resurfacing carries higher risk of pigment loss and scarring than erbium lasers. Recovery is longer than for gentler lasers, and darker skin tones and people with a history of cold sores or poor healing should discuss this with the provider.

chain: Smoother scars and fewer deep wrinkles
angle.text: Fractional CO2 vaporizes microscopic columns of skin, and deep collagen remodeling follows, smoothing scars and deep wrinkles over a longer recovery. It is the more intensive fractional laser and has the larger research base, including randomized trials.

lead: Fractional CO2 laser resurfacing uses a 10,600 nm carbon dioxide laser, invented by C. Kumar N. Patel at Bell Labs in 1964 [1], in a fractional pattern that vaporizes microscopic columns of skin while leaving tissue between them intact. Commercial systems include CO2RE, UltraPulse and SmartXide.

It is used in dermatology for acne scars, wrinkles, burn and surgical scars, and other conditions; published studies include burn-scar cohorts, acne scar studies in Asian patients and randomized trials combined with other therapies [2][3][4][2]. Wikipedia notes that CO2 resurfacing carries higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring than erbium lasers [5]. The same device class has also been studied for vaginal atrophy, outside the appearance focus of this wiki [6][7].
infobox: 1964, C. Kumar N. Patel, Bell Labs [1]

paras: A large prospective before-and-after cohort reported remodeling of hypertrophic burn scars with long-term follow-up [3]. A randomized split-face study combined adipose stem cell exosomes with fractional CO2 laser for acne scars [4], and a randomized trial used fractional CO2 laser to intensify photodynamic therapy of actinic keratoses [8]. A review covers the role of CO2 and fractional CO2 lasers in dermatology [2].

Wikipedia states that CO2 resurfacing produces more heat than erbium lasers and so carries a higher risk of hypopigmentation and scarring; other reported complications include hyperpigmentation, acne and herpes outbreaks [5]. Downtime is longer than for non-ablative fractional lasers.

Controlled and cohort studies exist for scars [3], acne scars [4], and actinic keratosis [8]. Registered trials include acne scars in Asians (n=12) [9], cesarean-section scars [10], cleft-lip scars (n=120) [11] and melasma with topical agents [12]. Studies on vulvovaginal atrophy include a randomized trial against topical estriol [6] and pilot studies [7], noted here only as related uses of the device category.
